analysis.one_liner: Sheilds judges from paying attorney's fees and from court orders in civil rights suits over their official acts.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill in November 1991 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but it never came to a floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal civil rights law so that a judge — state or federal — who is sued over something done on the bench could not be ordered to pay the other side's attorney's fees, and could not be ordered by a court to stop a practice, except in narrow cases. Today, people who win such suits can make the losing side pay their legal costs, and courts can order judges or court systems to end unlawful practices. The bill would close both of those routes unless the judge acted far outside any legal authority. It cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee and was placed on the Senate's waiting list for floor action, but no vote ever happened and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Judges and court officers who face civil rights lawsuits over actions taken from the bench. It would spare them the risk of paying a plaintiff's attorney's fees and of court orders requiring them to change practices, and it would generally make suing a judge less useful and more expensive.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends federal civil rights law so a judicial officer cannot be made to pay costs, including attorney's fees, in a suit over an act done in a judicial capacity, unless the action was clearly in excess of the officer's jurisdiction [S3].
It also bars courts from issuing injunctions against a judicial officer unless a declaratory decree was violated or declaratory relief was unavailable [S3].
The CRS summary confirms the changes apply to both state and federal judges acting in their judicial capacity, with the same narrow exceptions [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People who sue over civil rights violations committed by judges. They would have to pay their own attorney's fees even when they win, and they could not get a court order forcing a judge or court system to stop an unlawful practice in most cases — leaving only money damages, which the bill does not touch.

drawbacks.text: The strongest case for the bill is judicial independence: letting successful plaintiffs collect attorney's fees from judges, and letting courts issue orders against sitting judges, could chill decision-making and entangle courts in managing other courts.

For ordinary people, the cost is real: the bill would remove the practical leverage of fee awards and injunctions, so a person whose rights were violated by a judge could win a case on paper yet walk away with no fee reimbursement and no court-ordered fix, unless the judge acted clearly outside all authority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protects a real value — judicial independence — but it does so by shifting the burden of civil rights enforcement onto the individuals least able to bear it. Fee-shifting is what makes civil rights suits feasible for ordinary people, and injunctions are often the only meaningful remedy against an ongoing unlawful practice. The exception for acts 'clearly in excess of jurisdiction' is narrow and would leave most judicial misconduct beyond the reach of fees or injunctions. On balance, the bill's protections run toward officeholders, not the public.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it favorably and put it on the Senate's calendar of bills awaiting floor action in November 1991, but no senator ever got a vote on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 13, 1991 by Senator Heflin with cosponsors from both parties, the bill was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee [S5].
It moved through the committee's subcommittee on courts and was ordered reported favorably without amendment on October 31, 1991 [S5].
On November 20, 1991 the committee reported the bill to the Senate, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders — the waiting list for floor action [S5].
Minority views were filed with the committee report, meaning some committee members of the minority party formally objected to the bill [S5].
The bill never received a Senate floor vote, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who might need to sue over civil rights violations by judges are better off, since the bill never became law and the existing remedies — attorney's fee awards and injunctions — remain available. Judges and court officers, who would have gained immunity from those remedies, are worse off.

industries.industry: Judges and court officers (state and federal)
industries.note: The bill would give judges protection from attorney's fee awards and injunctions in civil rights suits over their official acts. Their gain is the public's loss of an enforcement tool, since fee-shifting is what makes many such suits affordable.

industries.industry: Civil rights plaintiffs and the attorneys who represent them
industries.note: Winning plaintiffs could no longer recover attorney's fees from a judge except in extreme cases, and could rarely get a court order to stop an unlawful practice. That would make these cases much harder to bring and to win anything useful from.
